title: Joshua 13:8–14
context: Before the western allotments, the narrative recalls the land Moses had already given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh east of the Jordan, the former kingdoms of Sihon and Og (Numbers 21; 32). The section notes honestly that Israel did not drive out the Geshurites and Maacathites, and that Levi received no land, since the LORD’s offerings are its inheritance. Both traditions read these verses constructively as a record of God’s past faithfulness and the people’s mixed obedience.

verses.text: With him the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond the Jordan eastward, even as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them:
verses.arminianNotes:
The Reubenites and Gadites had already received their inheritance from Moses east of the Jordan. The narrative recalls Numbers 32.

Arminian readers see continuity between Moses’ and Joshua’s leadership. What Moses granted is honored.
verses.reformedNotes:
Moses, ‘the servant of the LORD,’ assigned the eastern land. Joshua confirms what was already given.

Reformed readers see God’s purposes carried forward from one leader to the next. Both traditions read this as shared ground about faithfulness to earlier commitments.

verses.text: from Aroer, that is on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the plain of Medeba to Dibon;
verses.arminianNotes:
The eastern territory runs from Aroer on the Arnon valley through the plain of Medeba to Dibon. The Arnon marks the southern edge.

Arminian readers see the details as a record of real places God gave his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list starts in the south and moves north. Place names anchor the promise in actual geography.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness made concrete in specific towns and borders. Both traditions read this constructively as shared ground, holding some location details with caution.

verses.text: and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, to the border of the children of Ammon;
verses.arminianNotes:
All the cities of Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon, up to the Ammonite border, are included. Sihon’s defeat is told in Numbers 21:21–31.

Arminian readers see past victories remembered as a basis for present trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sihon’s kingdom becomes Israel’s inheritance. God turned opposition into a gift.

Reformed readers see God’s past acts as pledges of future faithfulness. Both traditions share this reading, with Sihon and Og often recalled in Israel’s praise (for example, Psalm 136:19–20).

verses.text: and Gilead, and the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan to Salecah;
verses.arminianNotes:
Gilead, the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, Mount Hermon, and Bashan to Salecah are listed. The territory extends north.

Arminian readers see the scale of what God had already given east of the Jordan.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list reaches up to Hermon and Bashan. The eastern land is wide.

Reformed readers see generous provision from God. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and both note that the Geshurites and Maacathites reappear in verse 13 as peoples Israel did not drive out.

verses.text: all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (who was left of the remnant of the Rephaim); for Moses attacked these, and drove them out.
verses.arminianNotes:
All of Og’s kingdom in Bashan, ruling from Ashtaroth and Edrei, is included; Og was of the remnant of the Rephaim. Moses defeated and drove them out.

Arminian readers see God giving victory over formidable opponents. Deuteronomy 3:1–11 tells of Og.
verses.reformedNotes:
The mention of the Rephaim stresses Og’s formidable reputation. Yet God gave Israel victory.

Reformed readers see God’s power over every opponent. Both traditions read this as shared ground, encouraging trust as Israel faces the land that remains.

verses.text: Nevertheless the children of Israel didn’t drive out the Geshurites, nor the Maacathites: but Geshur and Maacath live within Israel to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel did not drive out the Geshurites and Maacathites; they still live within Israel ‘to this day.’ The record is honest.

Arminian readers see incomplete obedience having real and lasting effects. The promise did not remove Israel’s responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator notes what was left undone. Geshur later appears in David’s family history (2 Samuel 3:3).

Reformed readers see God’s purposes advancing despite his people’s failures. Both traditions read this honestly and agree that the verse reports a failure without explaining it in detail.

verses.text: Only he gave no inheritance to the tribe of Levi. The offerings of the LORD, the God of Israel, made by fire are his inheritance, as he spoke to him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Levi receives no land; the LORD’s offerings made by fire are their inheritance, as God said. Their support comes from Israel’s worship.

Arminian readers see the Levites’ dependence on God and on the people’s faithful giving.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Levites’ portion is tied to the altar. Numbers 18:20–24 and Deuteronomy 18:1–2 set this out.

Reformed readers see a calling that rests on God’s provision rather than land. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, and Christians often draw lessons about supporting those who serve.
